title: How to use tax-loss harvesting in a US taxable brokerage account
description: Turning market losses into a tax asset to boost after-tax returns.
content:
No investor likes seeing red in their portfolio. However, in the US tax system, a financial loss can be converted into a tax asset. **Tax-Loss Harvesting (TLH)** is the practice of selling an investment that has lost value to 'realize' the loss, and using that loss to offset capital gains tax or ordinary income tax. It is the silver lining of a bear market. When done correctly, TLH can increase your after-tax returns by 0.50% to 1.00% annually without changing your portfolio's risk profile. This guide explains the mechanics and the 'Wash Sale' trap to avoid.

Key Takeaways

  • The Deduction Limit: You can use capital losses to offset unlimited capital gains. If you have net losses left over, you can deduct up to $3,000 against your ordinary income (wages) per year.
  • Stay Invested: The goal isn't to sell and go to cash. The goal is to sell, bank the tax deduction, and immediately buy a similar (but not identical) asset to catch the rebound.
  • The Wash Sale Rule: If you buy the 'substantially identical' security within 30 days before or after the sale, the IRS disallows the loss. You must swap to a different ticker (e.g., VTI to SCHB).
  • Tax Deferral: TLH effectively defers taxes into the future. You lower your tax bill today, which keeps more money compounding for you.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Robo-advisors (Betterment/Wealthfront) popularized automated TLH, but you can do it yourself at Fidelity or Schwab for free. It only applies to Taxable Brokerage Accounts. You cannot harvest losses in an IRA or 401(k).

The Harvesting Mechanics

Let's walk through a real-world scenario during a market correction.

The Scenario

You bought $10,000 of the S&P 500 (VOO) in January. By June, the market drops 10%. Your position is worth $9,000. You have a $1,000 unrealized loss.

The Execution

  1. Sell VOO: You sell all shares for $9,000. You have 'booked' a $1,000 capital loss.
  2. Buy a Partner Fund: Immediately take the $9,000 cash and buy a Total Market Fund (VTI). It performs almost identically to VOO (99% correlation), so you don't miss the recovery.
  3. The Result: You still have $9,000 invested in US stocks. But come tax time, you get a $1,000 deduction.

The Benefit

If you are in the 24% tax bracket, a $3,000 deduction saves you $720 in cold hard cash on your tax bill. That is an immediate return on investment just for clicking a few buttons.

Avoid the Wash Sale

  1. Don't Buy the Same Ticker: You cannot sell VOO and buy VOO. You cannot even sell VOO and buy SPY (another S&P 500 fund). The IRS considers them identical.
  2. The 'Substantially Identical' Test: Swap an S&P 500 fund for a Total Market fund (VTI). Or swap a Total International fund (VXUS) for an Emerging Markets fund (VWO). Change the index slightly.
  3. Check Dividend Reinvestment: If you sell VOO for a loss, but your account automatically buys $50 of VOO via a dividend reinvestment 2 days later, you triggered a Wash Sale. Turn off DRIP in taxable accounts.
  4. Don't Wait for December: Harvest losses whenever they happen. Volatility creates opportunities year-round.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does this reset my holding period?

Yes. When you buy the new fund (VTI), the clock resets for Long-Term Capital Gains. You must hold the new fund for 1 year to get the lower tax rate again.

Can I use losses from 5 years ago?

Yes. Capital losses carry forward indefinitely. If you lost $50,000 in 2022, you can deduct $3,000/year for ~17 years.

Is it worth it for small losses?

Generally, wait until the loss is at least $500 or $1,000. The effort/paperwork isn't worth it for a $50 deduction.
